analysis: All changes are documentation only. docs/developer/test.md (head only) describes test procedures: provider endpoint resumption/logout, App Attest dispatch, native serving qualification, checkpoint storage, release tests. It introduces no behavior change and does not contradict TB-011, T-053 or T-041. docs/operations/model-migration.md changes step 1 to allow reusing an already-published valid upload and skipping R2 write credentials. It also rewrites the HandleRegisterModel description (head lines 142-145) from 'verifies every listed file exists with declared size and hash' to 'validates identity and declared inventory, checks listed file sizes; providers verify hashes at download'. I flagged this as a low finding: the coordinator-side hash check appears to have been dropped, so the weight-hash chain (T-027/T-012, A-004) now relies on provider-side verification. The backend code is not visible here, so this is unverified. docs/operations/model-revisions.md was supplied as metadata only, with no text, so the referenced '#choose-the-operation-first' anchor and its access checks were not reviewed. The next pass should read model-revisions.md and the platform register handler to confirm the real verification behavior. Other threat IDs (TB-002, TB-003, T-041) were considered, but the reviewed text creates no new exposure.

findings.detail: The runbook previously said HandleRegisterModel verified that every listed file exists with the declared size and hash. It now says the handler only validates identity and declared inventory and checks listed file sizes, and that providers verify hashes at download time. Step 1 also lets operators skip upload and reuse an already-published manifest. A mismatched, corrupted or substituted object under the CDN prefix could then be registered and promoted with no coordinator-side content check. The alias fan-out would push that build to the fleet, and each provider's hard-swap is the only point where the bytes are checked. The trigger is a publishing mistake or CDN/R2 tampering. The impact is fleet-wide failed prefetches and retry load, or a stale or incorrect weightHash in the catalog. A malicious provider could also exploit a weak catalog hash to pass the weight-hash routing gate (T-027, T-012, SEC-007). The threat model and A-004 notes still describe coordinator weight-hash verification and have not been updated. The fix is to update the threat model, or restore hash verification at registration. Otherwise the runbook should require a pre-register hash audit and a single-provider canary before any promote or alias flip.
findings.title: Registration no longer documented as verifying file hashes; integrity rests on provider-side checks
